items.t: Hong Kong Stocks Tumble 370.95 Points As Tech Selloff Drags Hang Seng Below 24,000
Hang Seng falls 1.55% to 23,637.60 as tech stocks slide
sum: The Hang Seng closed at 23,637.60 points on Friday, November 13, down 370.95 points or 1.55 percent from Thursday's close of 24,008.55. MarketWatch listed the index as closed at 4:08 p.m. Hong Kong time, providing both the session close and the previous-session comparison in its Hang Seng Index data.

The decline was broad across major technology names and AI-related hardware companies. The Hang Seng Tech Index fell 3.02 percent to 3,813.19 points, according to Xinhua. The report also put the Hang Seng China Enterprises Index at 7,937.53 points, down 1.48 percent.

Large-cap technology stocks were among the main areas of weakness. Longbridge's Friday market wrap reported declines of 3.47 percent for Alibaba, 3.06 percent for Tencent and 3.74 percent for Xiaomi. It also said AI hardware and semiconductor names led the retreat, with Kingboard Laminates down 8.25 percent and Yangtze Optical Fibre and Cable down 7.28 percent. The detailed Longbridge market wrap attributed the pressure to concerns surrounding advanced AI-chip access and the global AI hardware supply chain.

The market's weakness was not uniform across sectors. Longbridge reported that PetroChina rose 2.79 percent to 10.33 Hong Kong dollars, while CNOOC finished unchanged at 22.84 Hong Kong dollars. Pork-related shares also attracted buying, although these gains were not enough to offset the decline in technology, semiconductor and new-energy-vehicle stocks.

For investors monitoring regional risk appetite, Friday's move brought the benchmark below 24,000 points and left the index 1.55 percent lower on the session. The official closing figure and sector-index data were also reported by Xinhua in its November 13 market summary.

sum: HONG KONG: Chinese stocks snapped a three-day advance while Hong Kong stocks dropped on Thursday, dragged down by market caution as investors assessed the potential fallout from a scandal involving US chipmaker Nvidia’s chief executive.
China’s blue-chip CSI 300 Index closed down 0.8 percent and the Shanghai Composite Index fell 0.7 percent.
Hong Kong’s benchmark Hang Seng declined 1.3 percent, while the Hang Seng Tech dropped 2.4 percent.
Investors worry Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s scandal could weigh on the business outlook of the US chip giant’s clients.

Hang Seng Index heavyweight Alibaba Group tumbled 7 percent, logging its biggest daily loss since August, as concerns mounted that cloud operators’ access to advanced chips could face tighter US restrictions.

“Tighter US chip restrictions could accelerate domestic semiconductor substitution while making it harder for Chinese cloud companies to access advanced computing technology,” Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo, said in a note.
Large language model startups Z.AI and Minimax lost 9 percent and 8 percent respectively.

sum: Акции Alibaba Group Holding в четверг упали на 7,3%, что оказало давление на индекс Hang Seng Tech, поскольку росли опасения, что Вашингтон может более пристально следить за доступом Китая к передовым чипам искусственного интеллекта.

Пострадали и коллеги из китайской индустрии искусственного интеллекта. Разработчики моделей Z.ai и MiniMax Group потеряли как минимум 8%. По данным Bloomberg, инвесторы опасаются, что Вашингтон может ужесточить меры в отношении того, как поставщики облачных услуг получают высококлассные чипы, поскольку разгорается скандал с участием генерального директора Nvidia $NVDA Дженсена Хуанга.

По данным Bloomberg, Alibaba арендует чипы Nvidia через сингапурскую компанию Megaspeed International. По данным CNBC, Дженсен Хуанг признался, что изменял своей жене после того, как сообщения связали его с Элис Хуанг, которая имеет связи с Megaspeed. По данным CNBC, представители американской разведки подозревают, что она работает в качестве агента китайской разведки. По данным The Japan Times, Китай отверг эти обвинения. Megaspeed отвергла обвинения в незаконной перенаправлении чипов в Китай.

По данным The Japan Times, Алиса Хуанг инвестировала и вела дела с рядом ведущих китайских технологических компаний, таких как Alibaba и Tencent. Корпоративные записи Сингапура показывают, что Apex Enterprise Solutions, подразделение Alibaba, вложила деньги в Speedmatrix, малазийскую компанию, связанную с Megaspeed.

По данным The Japan Times, китайские компании, занимающиеся искусственным интеллектом, стремятся арендовать вычислительные мощности на базе чипов Nvidia в центрах обработки данных, расположенных за границей. Один крупный китайский поставщик облачных услуг заранее обсудил возможность обеспечения мощностей за рубежом, в то время как более мелкие лаборатории искусственного интеллекта рассматривают аналогичные шаги.

По данным The Japan Times, компании обеспокоены тем, что это дело может дать новый импульс Закону о безопасности удаленного доступа. В соответствии с предлагаемым законом Министерство торговли США будет иметь право контролировать удаленный доступ к ограниченным технологиям через облако. Палата представителей одобрила его в январе 369 голосами против 22, а Сенат еще не принял по нему решения.

Джулия Пан, аналитик UOB Kay Hian, сказала, что китайские поставщики облачных услуг наращивают запасы чипов с января, но сроки исследований и разработок «неизбежно будут отложены», согласно Bloomberg.

China Resources Mixc Lifestyle stock joins UOB Kay Hian buy list
sum: UOB Kay Hian added 01209.HK, labeled China Resources Land Life in the featured recommendations, to its buy list in a report published on Thursday, November 5, according to AASTOCKS. The bank assigned the company a target price of 55 Hong Kong dollars.

UOB Kay Hian said Chinese equities had weakened further in October, with the Hang Seng Index and MSCI China Index declining 5.4 percent and 7.2 percent month on month, respectively. The bank expects volatility to persist in November but said stronger policy support increased the probability of a market bottom during the month.

The report cited measures including a 100 billion yuan securities firm and fund swap facility and a lower relending rate for share buybacks. It also pointed to strong weekly inflows into broad-based A-share exchange-traded funds as a supportive factor.

The inclusion places China Resources Mixc Lifestyle among the Hong Kong-listed companies that UOB Kay Hian expects to benefit if Chinese market sentiment stabilizes. The report also set stop-losses for its selected positions, underlining the bank's expectation that volatility remains a material risk.

China Resources Mixc Lifestyle describes itself as a leading provider of property management and commercial operational services. Its activities center on managing properties and operating commercial assets. The company is based in China and focuses on services connected with property and retail operations.

Stock Futures Tick Up as Traders Await Inflation Data and AI Earnings
sum: Stock futures demonstrated a slight uptick on Sunday evening as traders remained focused on the potential recovery of technology shares. Anticipation was building for the upcoming inflation data and earnings reports from major artificial intelligence companies scheduled for the week ahead. Specifically, S&P 500 futures recorded a gain of 0.1%, while the Nasdaq 100 futures increased by 0.3%. Additionally, futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average saw an increase of 101 points, equivalent to 0.2%.

Over in Asia, markets exhibited mostly positive performance on Monday, with Taiwanese equities leading the charge. The Taiwan Weighted Index surged nearly 5%, buoyed by a significant rebound in key stocks such as TSMC and Hon Hai Precision Industry, widely recognized as Foxconn. The Nikkei 225 in Japan climbed by 3.25%, while the Topix index increased by 3.44%, largely supported by gains in financial and consumer cyclical stocks. South Korea’s Kospi index rose by 1.15%, overcoming an initial decline, whereas the small-cap Kosdaq index dipped by 0.23%. Major tech companies Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix experienced gains of 2.49% and 2.03%, respectively. In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng Index rose 1.03%, while the CSI 300 index in mainland China was up by 0.3%.

Investors in Asia were also focused on October inflation data from China, which revealed the producer price index reaching its highest point in over four years at 5.7%. In contrast, consumer inflation came in slower than anticipated at 0.7%. Meanwhile, Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 faced a decline of 0.51%.

The preceding Friday had witnessed a partial rebound from Thursday’s significant selloff driven by AI-related concerns, as chip stocks experienced renewed buying interest. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite rose by 1.09% to 24,579.42, and the broad-market S&P 500 increased by 0.31% to 7,376.86. Conversely, the blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average fell by 237.33 points, or 0.46%, ending at 51,285.73. Broader investor sentiment remained cautious amidst stronger-than-expected jobs data, and concerns persisted following robust midterm election results for Democrats.

The Shanghai Composite fell as much as 1.07% at the open, and the ChiNext Index dropped 2% early on, before all three major stock indices rebounded collectively. The ChiNext Index extended its intraday gain to more than 3%, the Shenzhen Component Index rose over 2%, and the STAR 50 and STAR Composite Index gained more than 4% in early trading at one point. More than 4,700 stocks across the Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing markets advanced, as market sentiment shifted rapidly from panic to broad-based gains.

Hong Kong stocks performed even more strongly. The Hang Seng Index opened 1.66% higher and continued to climb, with intraday gains reaching 3.1% at one point; the Hang Seng Tech Index rose 1.43% early on before extending gains to more than 5%. Tech and internet stocks led the advance, with NetEase, Meituan and Xiaomi each up more than 8%, Alibaba up about 6%, and Tencent Holdings up over 5%.

Nikkei, Kospi crash up to 4.5% as investors see Democratic win in US midterms
sum: Major indices in Asia fell to their lowest in over six months on November 4 as key technology stocks declined amid early indications of a Democratic win in the US midterm elections, which could slow down artificial intelligence spending in Asia's tech-heavy markets. Among indices, Japan's Nikkei 225 fell the most and was down over 4% while the broader Topix First Section fell nearly 2%.

The MSCI Asia Pacific Index dropped as much as 2.3%, with the technology sector leading the decline. South Korea’s Kospi swung to a loss of 4% after being up as much as 3.2%. Stocks in Taiwan and Japan also declined. Singapore’s benchmark was poised to enter a correction.

Investors see a Democratic wave ushering in tighter regulatory scrutiny, particularly of artificial intelligence companies. This adds to an already difficult stretch for Asian equities as concerns grow whether the billions of dollars being poured into AI-related firms will generate sufficient returns.

“The prospect of stronger Democratic control in Congress is adding another layer of uncertainty to Asian markets,” said Dilin Wu, a strategist at Pepperstone Group Ltd. “AI regulation, chip export restrictions, and data centre energy policies could all be affected by the election outcome.”
In Japan, semiconductor-linked stocks fell, with Kioxia Holdings Corp. and Advantest Corp. down over 11% and nearly 8%, respectively, while shares of Tokyo Electron fell nearly 6%.

South Korea's Kospi index reversed opening gains and fell nearly 3.5% as key technology stocks fell. Kospi heavyweights Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix fell nearly 2% and over 3%, respectively. "Asia's AI infrastructure players are heavily exposed to US-led AI investment. If Democrats gain control of both the chambers of Congress, demand for greater oversight of AI could intensify, creating uncertainty over the timelines for data-center expansion," iM Securities Analyst Yang Hyun-kyung told Dow Jones.

China's CSI 300 and Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index fell marginally. Technology stocks fell in Hong Kong, with the sectoral Hang Seng TECH Index down over 1%. Shares of Hang Seng majors Alibaba Group Holding and Xiaomi Corp. fell over 2% each. In Australia, the S&P ASX 200 Index fell marginally.

sum: Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index rose 0.42% to 23,393.32 on Monday 2 November 2026, its second straight gain, as the Hang Seng Tech Index surged 2.25% led by Xiaomi, CATL, Alibaba and Tencent, while banks and gold miners lagged.

The Hang Seng Index, the main benchmark of the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, closed at 23,393.32 on Monday, up 98.90 points or 0.42%, according to Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing data reported by Xinhua and The Standard. It followed Friday's 1.5% rebound and marked the index's first session of November in positive territory.

The index traded as high as 23,543.30 but gave back part of those gains in the afternoon. The more significant move came in technology: the Hang Seng Tech Index jumped 2.25% to 3,839.41 after rising as much as 3% intraday, while the Hang Seng China Enterprises Index added 0.56% to 7,906.11. Full-day turnover reached HK$204.84 billion.

Two forces supported the market. First, expectations of fresh policy support in mainland China lifted sentiment, after regulators met banks and brokers to discuss stabilising the equity market and the People's Bank of China signalled a new liquidity operation. Chinese brokerage stocks were among the leaders as investors bet on higher trading volumes.

Second, easing oil prices and a recovery in US stock futures after Friday's technology sell-off gave investors confidence to buy back into beaten-down tech names ahead of Apple's quarterly results. Even so, the gain in the broader Hang Seng was modest because banks and gold-related stocks, which had served as havens in October, were sold to fund purchases elsewhere.

Xiaomi was the best-performing blue chip, rising 6.1%, followed closely by battery giant CATL, which gained about 6% as lithium battery shares rallied. Among the heavyweights, Alibaba climbed 2.5% and Tencent advanced 2.2%, together providing a large share of the index's points gain.

Chipmakers also recovered. Hua Hong Semiconductor rose nearly 3% and SMIC added 1.5%. Casino operators climbed despite a decline in Macao's October gaming revenue, with Galaxy Entertainment up 3.7% and Sands China up 3.1%. On the downside, Bank of China and BOC Hong Kong were among the weakest constituents after their recent results, and gold miners eased.

China regulators act to support stocks after October slump, mainland media reports
sum: Chinese financial regulators are preparing to take action to stabilize the market after a sharp decline in A-shares during October, according to mainland media reports.

The reports said that the People’s Bank of China, the China Securities Regulatory Commission, and the National Financial Regulatory Administration will meet with major banks on Monday. The regulators are expected to discuss expanding capital market support tools, including optimizing special re-lending facilities for stock buybacks and share purchases.
The special re-lending facility is designed to help listed companies and major shareholders access low-cost funds to repurchase shares and bolster stock prices.
A-shares experienced a significant downturn in October, with major indices hitting new lows for the year.
The Shanghai Composite Index fell 1.44 percent to close at 3,599.00 points on the final trading day of October, dropping below the 3,600-point mark for the first time this year.

Growth and tech stocks led the slide, with the Shenzhen Component Index down 2.73 percent to 10,833.78, the ChiNext Index dropping 4.13 percent to 2,413.63, and the SSE Science and Technology Innovation Board 50 Index declining 4.66 percent to 1,421.31.

Declines were widespread across sectors, led by heavy sell-offs in tech and media shares. More than 4,600 stocks across the entire market recorded losses. Combined turnover on the Shanghai and Shenzhen exchanges reached 1.67 trillion yuan (HK$1.97 trillion) that day, up 117.9 billion yuan from the previous session.

sum: Hong Kong equities returned from Monday's Chung Yeung Festival holiday with a broad decline on Tuesday 20 October 2026, as the Hang Seng absorbed two days of global news, the unchanged Chinese lending rates and a fresh sell-off in technology shares.

The Hang Seng Index closed at 23,867.74 points on Tuesday 20 October 2026, down 319.09 points or 1.32% from Friday's close of 24,186.83, according to Xinhua and RTHK data. The Hang Seng China Enterprises Index fell 1.21% to 8,030.26, while the Hang Seng Tech Index dropped 1.52% to 4,045.91.

Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing kept its securities markets closed on Monday 19 October for the day following the Chung Yeung Festival, which fell on a Sunday this year. Tuesday's session was therefore the first chance for Hong Kong investors to react to China's third-quarter GDP data, Monday's rebound in US technology stocks and the People's Bank of China's loan prime rate decision.

The Hang Seng finished at 23,867.74, a loss of 1.32%, wiping out Friday's 0.52% gain. The index stayed in negative territory throughout the session, with selling pressure intensifying in the afternoon and no meaningful recovery into the close.

The close leaves the benchmark back below the psychologically important 24,000 mark. Reuters reported that the Hang Seng Tech Index touched a two-year low during the session, underlining the scale of the pressure on Hong Kong's technology sector.

The one-year loan prime rate stayed at 3.00% and the five-year rate at 3.50%, the 17th consecutive month without a change. Stronger-than-expected growth reduced hopes that Beijing would deliver additional stimulus.

China's economy grew 4.5% year on year in the third quarter, accelerating from 4.3% and beating the 4.4% consensus, driven largely by exports. Good news for the economy turned into bad news for markets that had been hoping for easier monetary policy. Regional weakness compounded the move, as Japan's Nikkei fell 1.30% and South Korea's KOSPI slumped 3.73% on concerns about AI spending and rising bond yields.

The external pressure behind Hong Kong's sharp decline stemmed from a chain reaction in global bond markets. The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield climbed to its highest level since 2002, while the 30-year yield hit a 24-year high. The UK 30-year gilt yield briefly breached 6% for the first time since 1998, and Japan's 10-year government bond yield had already risen above 3% in September—the highest since 1996—demonstrating that the rise in long-end rates is not unique to the United States. Elevated long-end yields push up financing costs for financial institutions and compress asset valuations, making this the core drag on the day's trading.

A vacuum in capital flows amplified the decline. The Stock Connect southbound channel was suspended from October 1 due to the mainland China National Day holiday and will not resume until October 8. Mainland A-shares are also closed through October 7. With southbound capital absent, Hong Kong stocks lost a crucial source of incremental buying.

sum: Over the past few years, investors who have struggled to chase "value for money" in the stock market have mostly tasted the bitterness of missing out. Those "quality stocks" with low valuations and solid assets were ignored, their share prices stagnant like dead water; in contrast, high-valuation stocks lacking earnings support and relying solely on hype soared sky-high, capturing both attention and wealth. This paradox of "the cheaper it gets, the less it rises" has left many questioning their investment philosophy. As the Mid-Autumn Festival approaches and lights illuminate countless homes, households are once again troubled by the task of selecting mooncakes. If the "value for money" of stocks is confusing, how should we evaluate the "value for money" of the mooncakes everyone loves? Behind both lies an identical blind spot and wisdom.

Every Mid-Autumn Festival, the market is flooded with a dazzling array of mooncakes, ranging from tens to hundreds of yuan per box. But frankly speaking, many people do not know how to choose mooncakes that truly offer "high value for money."

In my culinary dictionary, high value for money definitely does not mean "cheap." Rather, it refers to whether the craftsmanship, ingredients, and freshness justify the price. In my view, large chain bakeries that charge hundreds of yuan and rely heavily on advertising and packaging often offer the worst value. Conversely, mooncakes that truly deserve the label of "high value" must meet five criteria:

Just as no one likes buying pre-packaged bread from a supermarket with a shelf life of up to a month, chain mooncakes add preservatives to extend their shelf life. Without freshness, mooncakes lose their flavor.

Large chains prioritize production volume and sales, using machines for uniform pressing. The result is fillings that are compressed too tightly, leaving only a cloying sweetness or saltiness on the palate. In contrast, dedicated masters take the time to knead by hand, locking in multi-layered, soft, and smooth textures.

When you tear open the individual packaging of chain-store mooncakes, you often smell little aroma. Why? Because in mass production, to rush shipments, mooncakes are sealed in plastic bags before they have fully cooled.

Wall Street's AI Trade Is Quietly Rotating From Korea and Japan Into China
sum: Barclays and UBS say clients are buying China-linked derivatives because the old AI trade in Korea and Japan has become crowded, expensive and harder to chase.

Wall Street's hottest AI trade has found a new address. According to a Bloomberg report published September 6, trading desks at Barclays and UBS are seeing rising client demand for bullish options and swap contracts tied to China's CSI indexes. UBS's sales and trading desk noted on August 30 that the largest weekly derivatives flow in Asia came from bullish bets on the CSI 300 and CSI 500, including long swaps and upside option structures. That is real flow. It is not a conference-panel theory.

The trigger is simple. The original AI trade got crowded. South Korea's Kospi, carried by Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, had been one of the world's loudest AI benchmarks this year. Then the trade cracked. Investing.com reported in August that the Kospi fell 22% in July, its steepest monthly decline since the 2008 financial crisis, as investors questioned AI valuations and sold chip names. Bloomberg had also reported in July that the Hang Seng China Enterprises Index jumped 4.5% as the Kospi slid into bear-market territory. Money didn't disappear. It moved.

UBS likes the CSI 500. The bank has been pointing clients toward the index as an alternative AI bet built around mid- and small-cap Chinese firms with exposure to Beijing's push for domestic chip and hardware self-reliance. Barclays is seeing something similar, with more interest in call spreads on onshore Chinese indexes and clients positioning for a grind higher rather than a sudden surge. You don't need a heroic forecast to understand the appeal. If Samsung and SK Hynix have already priced in too much of the AI cycle, a cheaper Chinese basket starts to look useful.

This isn't just a bank-desk story. Value Partners, one of Asia's larger fund managers, began selling some Taiwanese and South Korean AI holdings in August 2025 and buying more Chinese hyperscalers listed in Hong Kong, according to a Bloomberg report carried by The Business Times.

sum: The Hang Seng Index is a widely followed benchmark that tracks large and liquid companies listed in Hong Kong, including many major businesses closely linked to mainland China. Its movements can provide useful insight into Hong Kong market conditions and investor sentiment toward parts of the Chinese economy.
🎯This guide explains what the HSI tracks, how it is calculated, what affects its performance, and its main strengths and risks.

The Hang Seng Index, abbreviated as HSI, is a benchmark that tracks large and liquid companies listed on the Main Board of the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. It is widely used to measure the overall performance and sentiment of the Hong Kong stock market.

The HSI was launched in 1969 with 33 constituents and a base value of 100, backdated to July 31, 1964. It later adopted free-float-adjusted market-cap weighting, while reforms introduced in 2021 aimed to expand the index to 100 companies. By June 2026, it contained 93 constituents.

The HSI is sometimes called “Hong Kong’s Dow Jones” because both serve as widely followed flagship stock-market benchmarks. Investors also use it to assess sentiment toward Hong Kong and businesses closely connected to mainland China.

Investors follow the Hang Seng Index because it is a leading benchmark for the Hong Kong stock market, one of Asia’s major financial centres. By tracking large and liquid Hong Kong-listed companies, it provides a quick view of broader market performance and investor sentiment.
✅Track the Hong Kong stock market: The HSI helps investors determine whether major Hong Kong-listed companies are generally rising, falling, or moving without a clear direction.

Hong Kong ELS Sanctions Delayed Again to August; Lotte Card Ruling Likely on 31st
sum: The final decision on sanctions against South Korean banks for the misselling of Hong Kong H-Index (Hang Seng China Enterprises Index) equity-linked securities (ELS) is expected to be pushed beyond this month into August. In contrast, sanctions against Lotte Card, which suffered a massive customer data breach last year, are likely to be concluded within this month.

According to financial industry and regulatory sources on the 27th, it is highly probable that the Hong Kong H-Index ELS sanctions will not be finalized at the Financial Services Commission's (FSC) regular meeting scheduled for the 31st. A financial authority official stated, "There are still issues that need to be discussed within the FSC, so the situation remains fluid."

The core issue is the amount of the penalty surcharge. Under the sanctions proposal sent by the Financial Supervisory Service (FSS) to the FSC, the combined fines for five banks—KB Kookmin Bank, Shinhan Bank, Hana Bank, NH Nonghyup Bank, and Standard Chartered Bank Korea—amount to approximately ₩600 billion (approximately $411.1 million). Within the FSC, opinions are reportedly divided on whether to maintain the FSS's original proposal or to further reduce the penalty amount.

The banking industry has strongly protested, arguing that imposing massive fines on top of the large-scale voluntary compensation already carried out constitutes "double sanctions." They also contend that the penalties are excessive because the fines are based on the total sales amount, whereas the banks only earned sales commissions.

The FSC is under pressure after losing a series of lawsuits this year between financial authorities and financial firms. It is also conscious that confirming a huge penalty could weaken the momentum for productive financial policies that require cooperation from the banking sector. However, these sanctions carry symbolic weight as the first large-scale penalty since the enactment of the Financial Consumer Protection Act in 2021 and could set an important precedent for future sanctions related to misselling, making a significant reduction burdensome.
Previously in May, the FSC rejected the FSS's initial sanctions proposal, which included fines totaling ₩1.4 trillion (approximately $959.2 million).

items.t: Hong Kong market faces pressure as HK$255 billion in locked shares expire in July
sum: The potential wave of selling poses an additional headwind for the city’s struggling equity market
[HONG KONG] Hong Kong’s underperforming stock market may come under renewed pressure as a large amount of shares frozen under restrictions tied to equities offerings become tradable next month.

At least HK$255 billion (S$41.8 billion) worth of stocks, either from initial public offerings or secondary share sales, will see their temporary lockups expire in July, the most for any month through the rest of this year, according to exchange data calculated by Bloomberg.

Separately, Goldman Sachs Group estimates that IPO-induced lockup expiries in the city will total US$274 billion in the coming year, marking a record for any 12-month period. Shares held by cornerstone investors of a Hong Kong IPO and existing shareholders won’t be available for public trading for a period of time, typically for six months or a year after the stock’s listing.

The looming expiries result from an IPO boom in the financial hub late last year and early this year, when technology firms rushed to capture the artificial intelligence investment frenzy. The potential selling pressure would be an extra headwind for Hong Kong stocks, which have lagged Asian peers such as South Korea and Taiwan that have led the global AI trade.

Pressured by China’s struggling economy and doubts on Chinese firms’ heavy AI spending, the city’s Hang Seng Index has fallen 3 per cent this year, versus an over 100 per cent surge for Korea’s Kospi gauge and the 57 per cent gain for Taiwan’s Taiex benchmark.

“Historical precedents suggest that equities typically experience moderate downward price pressure following lock-up expiration,” Goldman analysts including Si Fu wrote in a note dated on Jun 14. Such stocks tend to see a median decline of 4 per cent in three months and 7 per cent in six months after they become tradable, they added.

South Korea's FSS Slaps Five Major Banks with Over HK$3 Billion in Fines, Drawing a Line Under HSCEI ELS Mis-Selling Scandal
sum: The more than two-year-long controversy over the mis-selling of products linked to the Hang Seng China Enterprises Index (HSCEI) in South Korea has finally met with a heavy regulatory hammer. South Korea's Financial Supervisory Service (FSS) announced it has imposed fines totaling approximately 600 billion won (equivalent to about HK$3 billion, or roughly $383.0 million) on five banks: KB Kookmin Bank, Shinhan Bank, Hana Bank, NH Nonghyup Bank, and Standard Chartered Bank Korea. This marks a preliminary regulatory conclusion to a financial incident that involved tens of thousands of retail investors and resulted in losses amounting to trillions of won.

The final penalty amount represents a significant reduction from the preliminary estimates floated by the FSS multiple times over the past year. In the early stages of the scandal, market speculation suggested maximum fines could reach around 4 trillion won; by February of this year, the FSS had proposed a plan of approximately 1.4 trillion won. The finalized 600 billion won figure is only about 15% of the initial maximum estimate and half of the February proposal, indicating that the regulator ultimately adopted a relatively moderate punitive approach after a lengthy sanctions review process.
The Backstory: When the HSCEI Plunge Met Systemic Sales Failures

At the heart of this storm are Equity-Linked Securities (ELS) tied to the Hang Seng China Enterprises Index. These structured products typically promise higher coupon yields when the underlying index performs stably, but investors risk significant principal loss if the index falls below a specific threshold.

According to FSS investigation data, since 2021, South Korean banks and securities firms cumulatively sold approximately 19.3 trillion won worth of HSCEI-tracking ELS products. Among them, KB Kookmin Bank had the largest sales volume, reaching 8.2 trillion won, accounting for over 40% of the total.

However, in early 2024, the HSCEI experienced a sharp downturn, causing a large number of ELS products linked to the index to trigger loss mechanisms. The FSS confirmed in early 2024 that five banks and six securities firms engaged in "serious regulatory non-compliance and systemic failures" during the sale of these complex financial products.

sum: While global markets continue to take stock of the conflict in Iran and energy shocks following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index has been left largely unshaken from its two-year growth spurt.

The index was buoyed in recent days by China’s resilience in managing the ongoing energy crisis. Given that China is the world’s second-largest oil consumer, using 8.1 million barrels per day, surges in the cost of Brent crude have been a leading cause of concern for the country as leaders lowered their growth target for the year to 4.5 percent, their lowest rate since 1991.

At its peak, Brent crude rose to $119.50 per barrel, due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a shipping lane that had seen around 20 percent of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) passing through it.

But with Russia expressing a willingness to assist China in its oil challenges, the outlook for the Chinese economy has strengthened, and for many stocks the pressure has lifted. The war in the Middle East may have been a major disruptive factor for Chinese stocks, but it appears that the Asian powerhouse is performing exceptionally well in terms of domestic productivity.

The Hang Seng index responded by recovering much of its losses since the escalation in the conflict between the United States and Iran began on February 28. Following an encouraging GDP report for the first quarter (Q1) of 2026, the Hang Seng rallied to HK$ 26,185, marking a 10 percent recovery from its lowest level this year. The Shanghai Composite Index also climbed to 4,637 yuan.

The jump was attributed to data released by the National Statistics Bureau (NSB), which showed that the economy had expanded 5 percent in Q1, marking a significant improvement on the previous quarter’s 4.5 percent growth.
Crucially, China’s GDP for the three-month period beat average estimates of 4.8 percent, helping the country’s gross domestic product to increase by 1.3 percent on a quarter-on-quarter basis.

Yesterday, we noted that the Beijing Municipal Administration for Market Regulation met with 12 internet companies, including Alibaba’s Taobao, Trip.com, Meituan, JD.com, ByteDance’s Douyin, and Kuaishou, regarding the ongoing delivery price wars. Instant commerce subsidies have weighed significantly on companies' bottom lines, as adjusted net income and adjusted EPS have both cratered.

Equity strategists are stuck focusing on the MSCI China Index and earnings per share (EPS). One caveat is that Alibaba’s artificial intelligence (AI) capex has also been a factor in the steep fall in EPS. Ultimately, the restaurant delivery and instant commerce price war has affected investors’ perception of China investing, both explicitly through the individual companies' EPS declines and implicitly through the knock-on effect of strategists who focus on MSCI China EPS.

sum: HONG KONG, 28 January 2026 – The Hang Seng Index (HSI) leads movements in residential capital values by an average of 2.2 months, according to JLL's latest Hong Kong Residential Sales Market Dynamics released today. The lag largely reflects the lower liquidity of the property market and delays in transaction registration. The findings underscore the strong correlation between equity market performance and residential capital values.

Data shows that, since June 2020, the HSI and residential capital values have generally moved in tandem. However, their trajectories began to diverge in July 2024: while the HSI continued to rebound, residential capital values did not rise concurrently but instead recorded a markedly narrower decline, followed by a modest recovery beginning in August 2025. This pattern suggests that, despite differing magnitudes of volatility between equities and housing, their overall directional alignment has largely persisted.

Norry Lee, Senior Director of Projects Strategy and Consultancy at JLL in Hong Kong, said: "Reflecting the strong performance of the equity market, Hong Kong's residential sector is expected to see near-term support. Anticipated interest rate cuts from 2026 could further strengthen investor sentiment. However, historical trends indicate that housing prices typically lag, adjusting more slowly than equity markets. Although conditions are improving, the high level of unsold inventory and ongoing macroeconomic uncertainties continue to weigh on the pace of recovery, warranting a cautious outlook."

In 2025, the HSI rebounded by 27.8%. Average daily turnover on the HKEX rose to HKD249.8 billion, an increase of approximately 90% y-o-y. In line with the equity market's gains, full year transaction volume in the secondary residential market reached 42,292 units, representing an 16.9% y-o-y increase. Total considerations amounted to HKD299.0 billion, up 14.4% from the previous year.

Why Chinese dividend stocks are worth considering for 2026
sum: The stocks have consistently delivered attractive returns over the past five years – making them a good portfolio consideration.

A quiet, powerful engine of wealth creation has been humming along in recent years, largely ignored by the mainstream narrative. Tucked within Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index, which has gone through ups and downs over the past five years, a select group of stocks has delivered a masterclass in consistent performance in terms of decent price returns and dividend yields year after year: Hong Kong-listed high dividend Chinese state-owned enterprise (SOE) shares.

The poster children for this thesis are, perhaps counter-intuitively, the titans of China’s oil and gas sector. While the global energy sector is dismissed as cyclical and politically fraught, China’s state-owned energy giants have been financial powerhouses. They have generated an average dividend yield of nearly 6% – a number that warrants attention in a world of declining interest rates.

The story gets better. This group has registered annualized price return exceeding 20% over the past five years. This consistent upward trajectory in share prices, occurring even as the oil price itself has been volatile and largely on a downtrend, requires an explanation. How has this decoupling been achieved?

The answer lies in the SOE reform initiated by the Chinese authority. The old perception of bloated, inefficient state-run companies is outdated. Under a mandate from Beijing to enhance shareholder value, these entities have embraced a new era of corporate stewardship. Operational efficiency, including steady output growth, is no longer a buzzword but a key performance indicator. This relentless focus on organic growth, combined with rigorous cost-cutting, has created an insulating effect to mitigate the nearly 20% decline in oil prices year to date.

Simultaneously, the SOE’s commitment to shareholders is now explicit and accelerating. These are not companies hoping to return cash; they are companies programmed to do so. They have not only demonstrated a track record of steady dividend payouts, but also proactively revved up their future payout targets.
